Choosing a first process to automate

The best first automation project is rarely the most impressive one. A short checklist for picking a process that will actually pay back.

When a business decides to try automation, attention tends to go to the most painful process in the building. That is understandable, and often a mistake. The most painful process is usually painful because it is complicated, political or poorly defined, and those are the conditions under which automation projects struggle.

A better first project is modest, frequent and easy to judge. It builds confidence, exposes how your systems really behave and gives the team a working example to point at.

Four questions to ask

  • Does it happen often? A task performed many times a week repays effort far faster than a quarterly one.
  • Is there a clear right answer? If two experienced colleagues would handle the same case differently, settle the rule before automating it.
  • Is the input reasonably consistent? Variety can be handled, but every additional format adds cost and failure modes.
  • What does a mistake cost? Low-stakes errors can be corrected afterwards. High-stakes ones need a person approving each result.

Map it before touching any tools

Write the process down as it actually happens, including the workarounds. Sit with the person who does it. You will almost always find steps nobody mentioned, and occasionally find that the process can be simplified so far that automation is no longer needed. That counts as a good outcome.

Decide where people stay involved

Automation works best as a division of labour. Let the system gather, extract, check and prepare. Let a person approve, handle exceptions and own the result. Designing these hand-off points deliberately is what separates a dependable workflow from a demonstration that falls over on its first unusual case.

Measure something simple

Before starting, record how long the process takes today and how often it goes wrong. Without a baseline you will have opinions about whether the project worked, and no evidence. A stopwatch and a tally sheet for two weeks is enough.
